_meta.description: Golden evaluation QA set for the bundled sample corpus (sample_data/sample_lecture.pptx).
_meta.verification_method: Every answerable item's source_quote is a verbatim substring extracted directly from the deck via DocumentParser + TextCleaner (see eval/README.md for the extraction command). No fact in any ground_truth was invented or pulled from general SCM knowledge -- if it isn't in source_quote, it isn't in the deck. Unanswerable items were checked against the full extracted text of every slide (2-18) to confirm the topic genuinely does not appear anywhere in the corpus.

schema.question: string
schema.ground_truth: string (verified answer) or null for unanswerable items
schema.category: one of the categories listed above
schema.answerable: bool -- whether the corpus actually contains the answer
schema.expected_slides: list[int] -- slide numbers (1-indexed as in the source PPTX) the answer is grounded in; empty for unanswerable items
schema.source_quote: verbatim substring (or list of verbatim substrings, when the answer draws on multiple spans) from the extracted slide text supporting ground_truth, or null for unanswerable items
schema.notes: string or null -- extra context, e.g. why an unanswerable item is a hard negative

items.question: What is inventory?
items.ground_truth: Inventory is quantities of goods in stock, i.e., stock of raw materials and finished goods.
items.source_quote: Quantities of goods in stock, i.e, stock of raw materials and finished goods.

items.question: What are the three categories of manufacturing inventory?
items.ground_truth: Raw materials and component parts delivered from suppliers, work-in-process (WIP) inventory, and finished goods inventory.
source_quote: Inventory of Raw materials and component parts that are delivered from suppliers.
Work-in-process (WIP) inventory: Raw materials and component parts enter the production process
Inventory of Finished Goods: Stock of finished goods after the completion of the production process.

items.question: What is work-in-process (WIP) inventory?
items.ground_truth: Raw materials and component parts that have entered the production process.
items.source_quote: Work-in-process (WIP) inventory: Raw materials and component parts enter the production process

items.question: What is service inventory?
items.ground_truth: Tangible goods that support delivery of a service, such as medical tools in an operating room or soaps in a hotel chain, plus items sold as part of the service, such as hair products at a beauty salon.
items.source_quote: The tangible goods that support delivery of the service, such as medical tools in an operating room or soaps in a hotel chain. It also includes items sold as part of the service, such as hair products at a beauty salon.

items.question: Give an example of service inventory in a hotel.
items.ground_truth: Soaps in a hotel chain -- tangible goods that support delivery of the service.
items.source_quote: soaps in a hotel chain

items.question: Give an example of items sold as part of a service, per the deck.
items.ground_truth: Hair products sold at a beauty salon.
items.source_quote: items sold as part of the service, such as hair products at a beauty salon

items.question: What are the two reasons given for carrying inventory?
items.ground_truth: To protect against lead time demand (by holding safety stock), and to maintain independence of operations (by holding buffer stock).
source_quote: Protect Against Lead Time Demand Holding extra inventory (safety stock) to ensure you have enough products to meet customer orders while waiting for new stock to arrive from suppliers.

Maintain Independence of Operations Holding enough buffer stock (raw materials, work-in-process, or finished goods) to ensure production and sales continue uninterrupted by supply chain disruptions, vendor delays, or demand fluctuations.

items.question: What is the purpose of holding safety stock, according to the deck's 'reasons for carrying inventory'?
items.ground_truth: To ensure there is enough product to meet customer orders while waiting for new stock to arrive from suppliers -- protecting against lead time demand.
items.source_quote: Holding extra inventory (safety stock) to ensure you have enough products to meet customer orders while waiting for new stock to arrive from suppliers.

items.question: What does 'maintain independence of operations' mean in the context of inventory?
items.ground_truth: Holding enough buffer stock (raw materials, work-in-process, or finished goods) to ensure production and sales continue uninterrupted by supply chain disruptions, vendor delays, or demand fluctuations.
items.source_quote: Holding enough buffer stock (raw materials, work-in-process, or finished goods) to ensure production and sales continue uninterrupted by supply chain disruptions, vendor delays, or demand fluctuations.

items.question: What is cycle stock?
items.ground_truth: Inventory for immediate use, computed based on expected demand over a certain time period. Also called lot size inventory.
items.source_quote: Cycle Stock (Lot Size Inventory) Inventory for immediate use and is computed based on expected demand over a certain time period.

items.question: What is safety stock, as one of the types of inventory?
items.ground_truth: The extra inventory a firm carries to serve as a cushion for uncertainties in supply and demand. Also called buffer stock.
items.source_quote: Safety Stock (Buffer Stock) The extra inventory the firm carry to serve as a cushion for uncertainties in supply and demand.

items.question: What is anticipation inventory?
items.ground_truth: Extra stock acquired in advance of anticipated demand surges, seasonal spikes, or expected supply chain disruptions.
items.source_quote: Anticipation inventory Extra stock acquired in advance of anticipated demand surges, seasonal spikes, or expected supply chain disruptions.

items.question: What is pipeline inventory?
items.ground_truth: Goods that have been ordered and paid for but are still in transit from a supplier to a warehouse or, finally, to the customer. Also called transportation inventory.
items.source_quote: Pipeline inventory (Transportation Inventory) Goods that have been ordered and paid for but are still in transit from a supplier to a warehouse or, finally, to the customer.

items.question: What does MRO stand for, and what does it include?
items.ground_truth: Maintenance, Repair & Operating items -- supplies, consumables, and spare parts used to support daily production and facility upkeep without becoming part of the finished product.
items.source_quote: Maintenance, Repair & Operating Items (MRO) Supplies, consumables, and spare parts used to support daily production and facility upkeep without becoming part of the finished product

items.question: List the five types of inventory described in the deck.
items.ground_truth: Cycle stock, safety stock, anticipation inventory, pipeline inventory, and MRO (maintenance, repair & operating items).
source_quote: Cycle Stock (Lot Size Inventory)
Safety Stock (Buffer Stock)
Anticipation inventory
Pipeline inventory (Transportation Inventory)
Maintenance, Repair & Operating Items (MRO)

items.question: What is holding cost (carrying cost)?
items.ground_truth: Costs that vary with the amount of inventory held in stock, including storage facilities, handling, insurance, breakage, depreciation, taxes, and the opportunity cost of capital. It varies with the time period inventory is held.
items.source_quote: Costs that vary with the amount of inventory held in stock, including storage facilities, handling, insurance, breakage, depreciation, taxes, and the opportunity cost of capital.

items.question: What is ordering cost (setup cost)?
items.ground_truth: Costs involved in placing an order and procuring the item, including deciding order quantities and the clerical costs of placing, tracking, and receiving the order.
items.source_quote: Costs involved in placing an order and procuring the item and involves deciding on order quantities, clerical costs involved in placing the order, tracking the order, and receiving it.

items.question: What is shortage cost?
items.ground_truth: The cost that occurs when a firm runs out of stock, reflecting the consequences of not having enough inventory.
items.source_quote: Shortage costs occur when we run out of stock and reflects the consequences of not having enough in inventory.

items.question: What are the three types of inventory costs described in the deck?
items.ground_truth: Holding cost (carrying cost), ordering cost (setup cost), and shortage cost.
source_quote: Holding Cost (Carrying Cost)
Ordering Cost (Setup Cost)
Shortage costs occur when we run out of stock and reflects the consequences of not having enough in inventory.

items.question: How does lowering ordering cost affect holding/inventory cost?
items.ground_truth: Lowering ordering cost results in higher inventory (holding) cost, because the firm then has to carry more stock.
items.source_quote: Lowering ordering cost will result in a higher inventory cost as we then have to carry more in stock.

items.question: How does inventory holding cost change as the order quantity Q increases?
items.ground_truth: Holding cost increases with order quantity Q -- higher order quantities mean holding more inventory.
items.source_quote: Inventory holding cost increases with the order quantity, 'Q'. Higher order quantities mean holding more inventory.

items.question: How does ordering cost change as order quantity increases?
items.ground_truth: Ordering cost decreases as order quantity increases, because holding more inventory means ordering less frequently.
items.source_quote: Holding more inventory means ordering less frequently, so ordering cost decreases.

items.question: What happens to ordering cost when the order quantity is small?
items.ground_truth: Ordering cost increases, because holding less inventory means ordering more frequently (though holding cost is lower).
items.source_quote: A smaller order quantity results in a lower holding cost. Holding less inventory means ordering more frequently, so ordering cost increases.

items.question: What two basic questions do inventory systems need to answer?
items.ground_truth: When to order, and how much to order.
items.source_quote: ANSWER TWO BASIC QUESTIONS WHEN TO ORDER? HOW MUCH TO ORDER?

items.question: What is a fixed-order quantity system?
items.ground_truth: An inventory management method where a specific, pre-determined amount of stock is ordered automatically whenever inventory levels drop to a designated reorder point.
items.source_quote: An inventory management method where a specific, pre-determined amount of stock is ordered automatically whenever inventory levels drop to a designated reorder point.

items.question: In the hotel-chain soap example illustrating the fixed-order quantity system, how many soaps does the hotel order, and at what inventory level?
items.ground_truth: The hotel always orders 2,000 soaps (for which it gets a quantity discount), placed when the number of soaps drops to 300.
items.source_quote: it always orders 2,000 soaps, for which it gets a nice quantity discount, and the order is made when the number of soaps drops to 300

items.question: What is a fixed-time period system?
items.ground_truth: An inventory management method where inventory levels are checked at fixed time intervals T, and the quantity ordered varies. A target inventory level R is set, and an order is placed to restore inventory to R.
items.source_quote: An inventory management method where inventory levels are checked in fixed time periods, 'T', and the quantity that is ordered varies. The system sets a target inventory level, 'R', to be maintained.

items.question: In a fixed-order quantity system, what does 'Q' represent?
items.ground_truth: The constant, fixed quantity that is ordered each time.
items.source_quote: Quantity that is ordered with this system is constant or fixed, and is denoted by Q.

items.question: In a fixed-order quantity system, when is a new order placed?
items.ground_truth: When the inventory position (IP) drops to the reorder point (ROP).
items.source_quote: An order is placed when the inventory position drops to a predetermined level, noted as the Reorder Point (ROP).

items.question: What causes the inventory position (IP) to decrease in a fixed-order quantity system?
items.ground_truth: The constant demand rate 'd', by which the inventory position is reduced.
items.source_quote: The system assumes a constant demand rate of 'd' by which the inventory position (IP) is reduced.

items.question: What happens to inventory position (IP) when a goods shipment is received?
items.ground_truth: Inventory position is increased by Q when goods are received -- the inventory is replenished.
items.source_quote: Inventory position is increased by Q when goods are received the inventory is replenished.

items.question: Why can't inventory arrive the moment an order is placed?
items.ground_truth: Because there is a lead time (L) during which the firm has to wait for the order to arrive.
items.source_quote: Inventory cannot arrive the moment an order is placed, as there is a certain amount of Lead Time (L) during which we have to wait for the order.

items.question: What is the formula for order quantity Q in a fixed-time period system?
items.ground_truth: Q = R - IP (the target inventory level minus the inventory position).
items.source_quote: 'Q – order quantity' is the difference between the target inventory (R) and the inventory position (IP). Q = R – IP

items.question: In the fixed-time period worked example (hotel chain, lavender bath soaps), how often is inventory checked?
items.ground_truth: Every two weeks.
items.source_quote: A hotel chain uses a fixed-time period model to check inventory levels every 02 weeks for its inventory of lavender bath soaps.

items.question: In the fixed-time period worked example, what is the target inventory level R?
items.ground_truth: 5,000 soaps.
items.source_quote: The hotel has a target inventory level R = 5,000 soaps.

items.question: In the fixed-time period worked example, if the inventory position after two weeks is 2,800 soaps, how many soaps should be ordered?
items.source_quote: it would place an order for quantity: Q = R – IP = 5,000 – 2,800 =2,200 soaps.

items.question: What does EOQ stand for?
items.ground_truth: Economic Order Quantity.
items.source_quote: Determining Economic Order Quantity (EOQ)

items.question: What is Economic Order Quantity (EOQ)?
items.ground_truth: An inventory management technique that determines the optimal order size a company should purchase to minimize total inventory costs, including holding and ordering costs.
items.source_quote: Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) is an inventory management technique that determines the optimal order size a company should purchase to minimise total inventory costs, including holding and ordering costs.

items.question: What is Total Inventory Cost (TIC) composed of?
items.ground_truth: Total Ordering Cost plus Total Holding Cost.
items.source_quote: Total Inventory Cost (TIC) = Total Ordering Cost + Total Holding Cost

items.question: What is the formula for Total Inventory Cost (TIC) in terms of D, Q, S, and H?
items.ground_truth: TIC = (D/Q) * S + (Q/2) * H, where D is annual demand, Q is order quantity, S is ordering cost per order, and H is holding cost per unit.
items.source_quote: TIC = (D/Q)*S + (Q/2)*H

items.question: In the TIC formula, what does D/Q represent?
items.ground_truth: The number of orders placed per year.
items.source_quote: D/Q = Number of orders per year

items.question: In the TIC formula, what does Q/2 represent?
items.ground_truth: The average annual inventory.
items.source_quote: Q/2 = Average annual inventory

items.question: In the EOQ/TIC formula, what does 'S' represent?
items.ground_truth: Ordering cost per unit (per order).
items.source_quote: S = Ordering cost per unit

items.question: In the EOQ/TIC formula, what does 'H' represent?
items.ground_truth: Holding cost per unit.
items.source_quote: H = Holding cost per unit

items.question: How is the Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) mathematically determined from the TIC formula?
items.ground_truth: By minimizing Total Inventory Cost (TIC) -- taking the first derivative of TIC with respect to Q, setting it to zero, and solving for Q.
items.source_quote: Taking first order derivative of TIC with respect to Q, Set it to zero and Solving for 'Q'.

items.question: Before considering EOQ, how did Georgia's Florist decide its order quantity for orchids?

items.question: What question does the Reorder Point (ROP) answer?
items.ground_truth: When more inventory will be reordered.
items.source_quote: The Reorder Point (ROP) answers the question when more inventory will be reordered.

items.question: What is the Reorder Point (ROP)?
items.ground_truth: The specific, minimum inventory level that triggers a replenishment order for an item, ensuring stock is refilled before it runs out.
items.source_quote: A Reorder Point (ROP) is the specific, minimum inventory level that triggers a replenishment order for an item, ensuring stock is refilled before it runs out.

items.question: Conceptually, how much inventory should the reorder point cover?
items.ground_truth: Enough inventory to ensure that demand is covered during the length of the lead time.
items.source_quote: The reorder point would simply be enough inventory to ensure that demand is covered during the length of the lead time.

items.question: What is the formula for Reorder Point (ROP) under constant demand?
items.ground_truth: ROP = d * L, where d is the demand rate and L is the lead time.
items.source_quote: Reorder Point (ROP) = d * L

items.question: In Georgia Florists' ROP example, what is the weekly demand (d) and lead time (L)?

items.question: What is the Reorder Point (ROP) for Georgia Florists?

items.question: What is the key difference between a fixed-order quantity system and a fixed-time period system?
items.ground_truth: In a fixed-order quantity system, a constant, pre-determined quantity is ordered whenever inventory drops to a reorder point; in a fixed-time period system, inventory is checked at fixed time intervals and a varying quantity is ordered to restore inventory to a target level.

items.question: How do holding cost and ordering cost trade off against each other as order quantity changes?
items.ground_truth: As order quantity increases, holding cost increases (more inventory held) while ordering cost decreases (fewer, larger orders); as order quantity decreases, holding cost decreases but ordering cost increases (more frequent orders).
source_quote: Inventory holding cost increases with the order quantity, 'Q'.
Holding more inventory means ordering less frequently, so ordering cost decreases.

items.question: What is the difference between cycle stock and safety stock?
items.ground_truth: Cycle stock is inventory for immediate use, computed from expected demand over a period; safety stock is extra inventory carried as a cushion against uncertainty in supply and demand.
source_quote: Cycle Stock (Lot Size Inventory) Inventory for immediate use and is computed based on expected demand over a certain time period.
Safety Stock (Buffer Stock) The extra inventory the firm carry to serve as a cushion for uncertainties in supply and demand.

items.question: What is the difference between anticipation inventory and pipeline inventory?
items.ground_truth: Anticipation inventory is extra stock acquired ahead of expected demand surges or disruptions; pipeline inventory is goods already ordered and paid for but still in transit.
source_quote: Anticipation inventory Extra stock acquired in advance of anticipated demand surges, seasonal spikes, or expected supply chain disruptions.
Pipeline inventory (Transportation Inventory) Goods that have been ordered and paid for but are still in transit from a supplier to a warehouse or, finally, to the customer.

items.question: How do 'when to order' and 'how much to order' get answered differently in the fixed-order quantity system versus the fixed-time period system?
items.ground_truth: In the fixed-order quantity system, 'when' is answered by the reorder point (ROP) and 'how much' by the fixed quantity Q. In the fixed-time period system, 'when' is answered by the fixed interval T and 'how much' by Q = R - IP.

items.question: Why does a firm need both an EOQ and a ROP, rather than just one of them?
items.ground_truth: EOQ answers 'how much to order' (the quantity that minimizes total inventory cost), while ROP answers 'when to order' (the inventory level that triggers a new order, accounting for lead time) -- together they fully define an ordering policy under a fixed-order quantity system.

items.question: How does the choice of order quantity Q affect both inventory costs and order frequency, and how does EOQ resolve this trade-off?

EOQ is the order quantity that minimizes the sum of these two costs (TIC).
